# The Space Between Thoughts

I'm thinking about how strange it is to write without direction, to let words accumulate like snow on a blank page. There's something both liberating and terrifying about it—the freedom to go anywhere colliding with the paralysis of infinite possibility.

Right now, someone is probably laughing at something that isn't funny. Or maybe it is funny to them, and that's what matters. Humor is so personal, isn't it? What breaks one person open with joy leaves another staring blankly. I wonder what that says about us—that we can stand in the same room, hear the same joke, and experience completely different emotional weather.

The more I think about it, the more I realize how much of life is just translation. We're all trying to take what's happening inside our heads and make it real enough that someone else can touch it. Words are the best tool we have, but they're also terrible tools. They're like trying to catch water in a net. Something essential always slips through.

I've been wondering lately why people keep diaries. Is it to remember, or to make sense of things? Maybe it's to prove that we existed, that we thought these thoughts and felt these feelings on this particular Tuesday. There's something defiant about writing things down—a middle finger to impermanence.

My grandmother used to say that everything circles back. I didn't understand what she meant then. I think I might now. Not in a mystical way, but in the way that life genuinely does repeat its patterns. The same arguments, the same hopes, the same crushing disappointments, but with different people wearing the masks. We keep trying to solve the same problems our ancestors tried to solve, generation after generation. And maybe that's not a failure. Maybe that's just what being human means.

I've never been good at small talk. I find myself either saying nothing at all or diving straight into something too deep—opinions about mortality at a cocktail party, philosophical questions while waiting in line at the grocery store. People don't appreciate that. They want their interactions bite-sized and convenient. There's a skill to keeping things light, and I've never developed it.

The thing is, though, I think most people are desperate to be understood. We're all walking around with this ache to be truly seen, and yet we spend so much energy making ourselves smaller, safer, less embarrassing. We become palatable versions of ourselves. Edited. Curated. We are all influencers of our own lives now, carefully crafting the narrative, showing only the angles that look best in the light.

I read something once about how the internet has made us all into performers. Even in private moments, we're thinking about how the story would sound if we told it to someone. Some of us have become so practiced at this that we're not sure if we actually experienced the moment or just performed experiencing it. That's the real horror of technology, maybe—not that it connects us, but that it trains us to distance ourselves from our own lives.

But maybe I'm being too harsh. People have always been like this, haven't they? We've always told stories about ourselves. The internet just made it visible and permanent.

I've been thinking about regret. About how there are these moments in life where you can feel the divergence happening, where you know this is a choice that will matter. And sometimes you make the right choice and sometimes you don't, but the terrifying thing is that you can't know at the moment itself. You can only know backward, by living into the consequences.

There's a version of me where I made completely different choices. There's a version that's braver, one that's more cautious, one that finished that novel, one that stayed in that city, one that made that phone call. These versions all exist in the quantum foam of probability, and I'll never know what they became. Maybe that's mercy. Maybe ignorance isn't just bliss—maybe it's necessary.

What would you do differently, I wonder? If you could go back? Or would you do everything exactly the same, because changing anything means erasing yourself?

I think about children and how they ask so many questions. We say it's because they're curious, but maybe it's something else. Maybe they're desperate to map the territory of reality before they have to start pretending they already know things. Adults are so sure about so much, and I think it's mostly a bluff. We're all just pretending we understand how to be alive.

Here's something true that I don't say very often: I don't know how I got to be this age. I keep expecting to feel grown-up, and instead I feel like I'm still waiting for the adults to arrive. Turns out there are no adults. There's just people doing their best and hoping nobody notices they're making it up as they go.

I've always loved the hours right before dawn. There's something about that suspended moment when the night is ending but day hasn't quite begun. The world feels softer then. Possibilities hang in the air like dust motes. The day hasn't disappointed you yet.

Maybe that's what writing without direction is like too—existing in that space before meaning arrives. Just words, sentences, the shapes of thoughts before they crystallize into something rigid. Once you say something out loud, it becomes real in a different way. It can be argued with. It can be wrong. In the space before saying, everything is still true.

I don't know where this was supposed to go. I don't know what the point was supposed to be. But maybe that's not really the point anymore. Maybe the point is just the thinking, the writing, the small private act of attention we pay to our own minds and to each other.

Someone will read this and feel seen by some sentence they weren't expecting. Someone else will think it's self-indulgent garbage. Both things will be true. And that's strangely okay.
